text.p: German airline Lufthansa AG said its group net profit in 1996 was lower than the previous year's result of 1.47 billion marks despite solid gains in the number of passengers carried to the Asia, Africa and the Middle East.

Managing board member Hemjoe Klein told a news conference at the ITB world tourism trade fair in Berlin that the Lufthansa group carried 1.7 percent more passengers in 1996 to a total of 41.4 million.
Klein said the number of passengers in the parent company, however, fell 0.6 percent to 31.8 million.
The passenger seat load factor declined by 0.2 percentage points to 70.3 percent in the Lufthansa group, and by 1.0 points to 68.6 percent in the parent company.
Klein said the group's ability to hold the seat load factor over 70 percent was an impressive accomplishment.
"Compared to 1995 we were able to raise the group performance moderately," Klein said. "But the group net profit for 1996 is below the year earlier level."
He declined to provide any more precise profit figures for 1996, saying they will be published at the end of March.

Klein said Lufthansa's passenger volumes gained 5.7 percent to Asia, Africa and the Middle East, 4.8 percent to South America, 1.3 percent in Europe and 0.8 percent to North America. But passenger volumes in Germany fell 2.2 percent.

Europe still held the largest share of traffic in 1996 with 39.1 percent, followed by Germany with 20.6 percent, Asia, Africa and the Middle East with 20.6 percent, North America with 16.6 percent and South America with 3.1 percent.
"The developments in international traffic were positive last year," Klein said.
Klein said Lufthansa aims to continue cutting costs and hopes to achieve a goal of reducing unit labour costs to well under 15 pfennigs per offered seat-kilometre.

Klein said that Germany had "lost a great opportunity to show the world a new Germany" in the six years after German unification and said the country needed to greatly improve its services industries.

"The attractiveness of Germany has to be defined in the future more with culture and more modern services industries," he said. "The political and economic importance of the travel industry has to be made more clear to the public."
The number of incoming travelers to Germany climbed by 19 percent to 5.7 million between 1990 and 1996 compared to an 82 percent rise to 25.3 million outgoing travelers each year.

"We didn't take advantage of the chances we had," Klein said, adding Lufthansa would sign an agreement with the German Tourism Board (DZT) on Monday to contribute 3.25 million marks for more tourism marketing for Germany.
"There is certainly a lack of sunshine and beaches in Germany," Klein said. "But we are nevertheless convinced that we have to do more to strengthen the flow of tourism to Germany."

Germany had a trade surplus of 97.6 billion marks in 1996, but more than half of that surplus was eroded by a 51.1 billion deficit in the tourism sector. Germans spent 70 billion marks abroad last year compared to 18 billion marks spent in Germany by foreign travellers.
